added_claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
added_claims.quote: after so many years of loose monetary policy, massively loose fiscal policy, finally we had this inflation shock, which was a game changer
added_claims.claim: The COVID shock was external but triggered a massive central-bank reaction and asset inflation; after years of loose monetary and fiscal policy, goods and consumer inflation arrived in 2022, so loose policy sowed the inflation shock that ended the 'bad news is good news' regime.
added_claims.indicator: central bank easing, fiscal stimulus, inflation
added_claims.testable: partly - historical sequence, causal link is argued

added_claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
added_claims.quote: every developed central bank really became what's called dovish
added_claims.claim: In December 2023 the Fed and nearly every developed central bank (all except the BoJ) turned dovish while growth was decent, a benign backdrop for equities, and markets had already rallied in anticipation of it.
added_claims.conditions: Growth must be decent for easing to be bullish rather than a recession signal.
added_claims.testable: yes - equity returns around the pivot

added_claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
added_claims.quote: neither the Iranian attack nor the Israeli defense were true acts of war, was more like to calm down their own local populations
added_claims.claim: Pablo reads the April 2024 Iran-Israel exchange as largely symbolic, giving a short-term truce, but a line was crossed (direct attacks from each country's territory) and small war games can go wrong; a single mass-casualty strike would have forced a much harder Israeli response.
added_claims.conditions: Depends on miscalculation or casualties; the truce is short-term.

added_claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
added_claims.quote: a 1.2 peak headline PCE, that annualizes at 15%
added_claims.claim: The mid-2022 inflation peak was extreme on a monthly basis: headline PCE peaked at 1.2% in a month (15% annualised) and core near 8% annualised, in a world used to 2% inflation and deflation fears.
added_claims.conditions: Data point on the size of the 2022 inflation shock.

added_claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
added_claims.quote: We are really, really focused on global central banks, monetary policy, something that we can anticipate well. When central banks are in action, we typically perform really, really well.
added_claims.claim: A macro book's key inputs are growth, inflation and the Fed and other central banks; central-bank policy is the part it can anticipate well, and it performs best when central banks are actively changing policy.
added_claims.direction: macro returns higher when central banks act
added_claims.conditions: Weaker when central banks are on hold.
added_claims.testable: partly - macro index returns vs policy-change episodes

added_claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
added_claims.quote: We have very low correlation to asset classes in the long run, but on any given day, we proactively seek to have exposure to markets to profit from changes
added_claims.claim: Discretionary macro sits between passive/long-only tactical allocation and pure arbitrage: it has low long-run correlation to asset classes but takes active directional exposures day to day.
added_claims.indicator: macro style positioning vs asset classes
added_claims.testable: yes - correlation of macro index to asset classes

added_claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
added_claims.quote: rates needed to replace four, 500 basis points. When that happens, usually stocks go down.
added_claims.claim: In 2022 the macro book paired short global rates (on the view that rates needed to rise 400-500bp) with short stocks and short commodities and long the dollar, because large rate rises usually push stocks down and the Fed was the most aggressive central bank.
added_claims.direction: short rates, short stocks, long USD
added_claims.conditions: A regime of aggressive central-bank tightening.

added_claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
added_claims.quote: we are good at forecasting bad markets for equities. And typically we would get short in anticipation and during those markets
added_claims.claim: A macro manager claims no long or short bias but skill at anticipating bad equity markets, going short in anticipation and during them, and shifting risk-on exposure by regime.
added_claims.direction: short before and during equity sell-offs
added_claims.conditions: Self-reported; the 2020 sell-off shows it fails sometimes.
added_claims.testable: yes - macro index conditional correlation to equities

added_claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
added_claims.quote: This is the index we made more than double that.
added_claims.claim: In the 2022 equity drawdown (-25%) the macro index returned about 10% on average while Graham's own macro program made more than double that.
added_claims.indicator: Graham macro vs macro hedge fund index 2022
added_claims.conditions: Manager-specific record from a firm presentation.

added_claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
added_claims.quote: macro trades at the lower roll than equities. Secondly, it has almost zero correlation
added_claims.claim: Adding macro lowers portfolio volatility for two reasons: the macro index runs at lower volatility than equities and has almost zero correlation to the portfolio, so the Sharpe ratio rises (return up while volatility falls).
added_claims.conditions: Applies to a 60/40 portfolio with 10-20% macro.
added_claims.testable: yes - from index volatility and correlation

corrections.issue: Says equities rallied 'after the Fed turned dovish in December'. Pablo says the S&P bottomed around 4200 at the end of October and rose 1000 points in four months, and that the rally started before the Fed pivot (markets were reading it ahead of time).
corrections.fix: From a late-October 2023 low near 4200 the S&P rose about 1000 points in four months, in a near straight line with an information ratio near 4 in Q1 2024 versus a normal 0.6-0.7, with volatility at lows; the rally began before the Fed's December dovish pivot, so markets anticipated it.

completeness_estimate: 0.82 - first reader caught the headline themes, statistics and tables (central-bank regimes, vol, stock-bond correlation, drawdown record, 60/40 results); missed supporting mechanisms (post-COVID policy sequence, Middle East reading, macro style and vol reduction reasons) and misordered the Q1 2024 rally versus the Fed pivot.
